author: Aaron Montes
title: El Paso Water customers mostly paying for water infrastructure on fringes of city - NewsBreak
text:
By Aaron Montes Edith Montero ,
1 hours ago
EL PASO, Texas ( KTSM ) — El Paso Water’s budgeted $1.2 billion water and wastewater capital improvement projects are expected to be funded mainly by its customers, according to the utility’s officials.
As of Wednesday, April 15, the utility accounts for a combined $345.6 million in total costs, leaving $854 million needed to cover funding needed for the planned projects serving new communities on the fringes of the city.
During a Capital Improvements Advisory Committee meeting, Gustavo Hurtado, El Paso Water’s Capital Projects Manager, said developers have contributed $24.6 million to costs for new water and wastewater infrastructure in the Northwest, Northeast and Eastside. That is after the utility collected impact fees on 199 total subdivisions since May 12, 2009.
Impact fees are authorized by state law and allow cities to collect revenue from the charge to pay for capital improvements or facility expansions needed for new developments.
The latest numbers are reflected by impact fee collections as of February 28. Hurtado said when the utility cannot cover costs with grants or other revenue, planners look to ratepayers and bonds to pay for construction costs.
“We issue them [bonds] as we need them,” Hurtado said. “It’s going to go back to the ratepayers to help us pay off those debts.”
In May 2024, the El Paso City Council increased its impact fee to 28%, covering inflationary impacts, President John Balliew and CEO of El Paso Water said. The impact fee adjustment came after calls to shift more of the cost onto developers.
The vote came with opposition from builders who said the increase would shift cost onto new homebuyers and push investment outside the city limits.
Bobby Bowling, co-owner of Tropicana Homes, said that concern has become a reality. Bowling told KTSM 9 News more than half of homes built in El Paso County have done so outside the city of El Paso.
“The reality of it is about 98% of El Paso homeowners didn’t pay an impact fee. So, they came into the system, the water and sewer system for free,” Bowling said. “And, yet, the rate structure requires every rate payer to pay a portion of their rates every month to repair and replace dilapidated infrastructure. That’s not really fair.”
Bowling said there is a concern that increases in costs for new homes will push potential buyers to stay home longer or choose renting as a more cost effective option.
The largest projects driving costs for El Paso rate payers are the planned $173 million Pure Water Center and $605.1 million Bustamante Wastewater Treatment Plant expansion.
Impact fees won’t be reconsidered until at least 2028, when City Council is scheduled to revisit and set the rates again.
